notes.claim: When repeating gives a randomly different result, averaging more measurements generally gives a better estimate of the value.
When the same influence affects every repeated measurement, you learn nothing extra just by repeating the measurement.
The standard uncertainty of a mean of uncorrelated measurements is smaller than that of a single one, so the mean is buffered against random errors.
The error in an average of repeated measurements is the error in one measurement divided by the square root of the number of repeats.
A meter accuracy of plus or minus (2% + 2 counts) means a reading of 100.0 V can be anywhere from 97.8 V to 102.2 V.
An uncertainty needs two numbers, the width of an interval and a confidence level, for example 20 centimetres plus or minus 1 centimetre at 95 percent.

sources.title: Good Practice Guide No. 11
sources.quote: random - where repeating the measurement gives a randomly different result. If so, the more measurements you make, and then average, the better estimate you generally can expect to get.

sources.title: Good Practice Guide No. 11
sources.quote: systematic - where the same influence affects the result for each of the repeated measurements (but you may not be able to tell). In this case, you learn nothing extra just by repeating measurements.

sources.title: Uncertainty of Measurement: A Review of the Rules for Calculating Uncertainty Components through Functional Relationships - PMC
sources.quote: This is indeed why the mean is often used for summarising measurements: the mean is better ‘buffered’ against random errors than are any of the individual component measurements.

sources.quote: divided by the square root of the number of times the measurement was repeated.

sources.title: Why Digital Multimeter Accuracy and Precision Matter | Fluke
sources.quote: Accuracy may also include a specified amount of digits (counts) added to the basic accuracy rating. For example, an accuracy of ±(2%+2) means that a reading of 100.0 V on the multimeter can be from 97.8 V to 102.2 V.

sources.quote: For example: We might say that the length of a certain stick measures 20 centimetres plus or minus 1 centimetre, at the 95 percent confidence level.
